opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest reason is that it's useful for the people who come after you. When I was a student, I spent a lot of time on assignments where the instructions were unclear, the starter code was messy, or I had no idea what a good solution was even supposed to look like. If someone before me had put their work online, with some notes on what went wrong and how they fixed it, I could have spent that time on the parts that actually teach you something.

There's also a selfish side. If you know other people will read your code, you write it differently. You clean it up, you write a proper README, you think about structure instead of just getting it to pass the grader at 3 a.m. That habit carried over into how I work on real projects later. Open source, in a way, starts there: you learn to write things that someone else can pick up and use.

I know some people worry this makes cheating easier. I understand that, but I think the responsibility is on the student who copies, and partly on courses that reuse the same assignments every year without change. Students who want to learn will use it as a reference, compare approaches, and understand the material better. Students who want to copy will find a way regardless. Hiding everything mostly hurts the honest ones.

And honestly, it's a small way to give back. A lot of what I learned came from things other people shared for free online. Putting my own work out there felt like the natural thing to do.

r001.rationale: The response says that time spent wrestling with unclear instructions, messy starter code, or uncertainty about a good solution could instead have gone to parts that teach something.

r002.rationale: It says sharing past work could free time for more meaningful learning, but does not say it gives later cohorts more time for pursuits they want to undertake.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started pretty selfishly. When I was a student at Tsinghua, I'd finish a project and think, this took me three weeks and a lot of dead ends, and now it just sits in a folder on my laptop. That felt like a waste. So I put it on GitHub mostly so I wouldn't lose it, and so I'd have something to point to when people asked what I'd actually built.

But then other students started finding it, and that changed how I thought about it. Course assignments are a strange category of code. They're small enough to actually read end to end, which almost nothing in industry is. And they're solving a well-defined problem that thousands of other people are also trying to solve, often with no reference beyond a PDF and a TA who's busy. When I was stuck, the thing that helped most was seeing how someone else structured their solution, not copying it, just seeing that it was possible and roughly what shape it took. I wanted to give that back.

There's also an honest argument about accountability. If I know the code is going to be public with my name on it, I write it differently. I clean up the variable names, I write a README, I think about whether the thing actually runs on a fresh machine. That discipline carried straight into my later work. Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, started as something not that far from a course project, and the habits I'd built from publishing assignments are a big part of why it was usable by other people from day one.

I know the obvious objection, which is cheating. And I take it somewhat seriously. But I think the fix is on the course design side, not on the side of hiding knowledge. If an assignment can be defeated by searching GitHub, it was already fragile. The good courses I took were the ones where you could look at every public solution and still have to do the real thinking yourself. So on balance I think the openness does more good than harm, and I'd rather err toward sharing.

r001.rationale: The response mentions project dead ends and seeing how others structured solutions, but it does not say that prolonged time stuck yields little learning benefit.

r002.rationale: It says public solutions can help other students and that sharing does more good than harm, but it does not present sharing as giving later cohorts more time for pursuits they want.

astra-6.text: For me, the value is that learning doesn’t have to stop when you submit an assignment. If I share my work, someone working through a similar problem can see how I approached it, and they might point out a mistake or suggest a better solution. That helps both of us learn. I’d want to respect the course’s rules, of course—the goal is to share ideas and make discussion possible, rather than just give people something to submit.

r001.rationale: The response discusses sharing work to learn from feedback, but does not say that prolonged time stuck on an assignment yields little learning benefit.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention helping later cohorts save time for pursuits they want to undertake.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the value is that an assignment can be useful beyond just getting a grade. Sharing my work gives other students something to learn from, and it gives me a chance to get feedback and see different approaches. I’d want people to use it to understand the ideas and build their own solutions, rather than simply copy it.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions learning from shared work, feedback, and different approaches, but does not discuss prolonged periods of being stuck or the limited learning benefit of that time.
